newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian Congress weakens anti-drug legislation.
newsitem.headline: Colombian Congress weakens anti-drug legislation.

text.p: Two key committees of Colombia's Congress have rejected the government's call for prison sentences totalling up to 30 years for drug kingpins or anyone else convicted of leading a criminal enterprise.

Constitutional reform committees of the House and Senate turned down the measure late on Tuesday in a joint session called to debate legislation to stiffen penalties for drug lords or other top criminals and those who conspire with them.

The bill, submitted by the government in September, would have required prison sentences of 20 to 30 years for those found guilty of masterminding or financing criminal groups. The mandatory jail terms would have been in addition to separate sentences meted out for specific crimes such as drug trafficking, illicit enrichment or money laundering.
The congressional committees ruled that mob bosses were entitled to the same treatment as their foot soldiers, however, and should not be singled out for harsher treatment.

Government officials could not be reached for immediate comment on the move to take the teeth out of the proposed crackdown on criminals, including the heads of organisations responsible for kidnapping, extortion and terrorism.
A headline in Bogota's respected daily El Espectador appeared to say it all. "Law Custom-made for Capos," it said.

Committee members have dragged their feet on the measures since last week, signalling by failing to turn up for debates their unwillingness or fear of punishing powerful drug lords in the face of widely reported death threats and intimidation.

Passage of the legislation is considered key to the government's effort to avert the U.S. economic sanctions that diplomats say could be imposed on Colombia next March as part of Washington's annual drug certification process.

But government sources concede the legislation could be watered down to the point where it would do nothing to convince the administration of President Bill Clinton that Colombia is fully committed to the global fight against drugs.

Congress is set to adjourn on Dec. 16 and will not return until March unless the government calls an extraordinary session. As a result, the proposed law may not be scheduled for a vote in the full House and Senate before March.

The opposition Conservative Party added to that possibility on Wednesday by announcing it planned to boycott all sessions of Congress, effective immediately, to protest successful moves by Communications Minister Saulo Arboleda to block the opening of a congressional ethics probe against him.
